title: Where is your main water shutoff? Find and record it
dek: Trace where water enters, confirm the customer-operated valve, and record safe instructions. Shared supplies and fire sprinklers need extra care.
metaDescription: Trace where water enters, confirm the customer-operated valve, and record safe instructions. Shared supplies and fire sprinklers need extra care.

paragraphs: Look near where the water supply enters the home, such as a basement entry point, utility area, or another location identified in the property records. Then confirm that the valve controls your domestic supply and that you are allowed to operate it. Do not assume the nearest valve, water-heater valve, or curb box is the right one.

The best time to find it is before water is escaping. You need more than a photograph of a handle: you need the location, which supply it controls, safe access, and who to call if it will not work. In apartments, shared buildings, well systems, and homes with fire sprinklers, ask the responsible professional or manager before experimenting.

body.heading: Find and document the correct valve
items: Check the inspection report, plumbing records, or building information for the supply entry point.
Ask the landlord, building manager, utility, or plumber which valve serves your unit or house.
Follow accessible visible pipework only where it is safe to do so.
Confirm whether domestic water and fire sprinklers have separate branches.
Record which valve occupants may operate and which belongs to the utility or building.
Ask for a demonstration if its operation or condition is uncertain.
Photograph the confirmed location and write directions from a familiar doorway.
Share the record with appropriate household members and keep access clear.

body.heading: Use common locations as clues, not a guarantee
paragraphs: [WSSC Water's valve guide](https://www.wsscwater.com/customer-service/report-problem/find-and-operate-your-main-water-valve) describes several layouts, including valves near entry points, utility equipment, and other locations depending on construction. Its instructions concern its service area and typical arrangements there. They are not proof that every home everywhere has the same setup.

A valve beside a water heater may control only that appliance. A small valve under a sink may control that fixture. Trace and confirm the supply rather than labeling the first handle you find 'main.' If doing that would require opening walls or entering an unsafe space, stop and ask for help.

body.heading: Identify before operating
rows: It serves the intended domestic supply and is safe to use.
It isolates the specific sink, toilet, or appliance, not the whole home.
Your utility's ownership and permitted operating procedure.
The correct response without disabling protection unnecessarily.
Who is authorized and which other units would be affected.

body.heading: Invented example: two handles by the meter
paragraphs: A homeowner finds two valves near a meter and is unsure whether one also affects the fire sprinklers. Instead of following an online rule to turn the first handle, they ask a qualified plumber to identify the domestic shutoff. They record 'domestic valve confirmed by plumber, November 17' and keep a labeled photograph.

The record also identifies a separate valve that must not be treated as the everyday domestic control. The point is not that two handles always mean the same layout. It is that the actual configuration must be understood before a rushed choice.

body.heading: Learn the actual operation, not just a handle stereotype
paragraphs: Wheel and lever handles often have different operating actions, but appearance alone is not enough to justify forcing an unfamiliar valve. Have the correct valve and direction confirmed. Record any instruction about closing slowly, stopping position, and restoring service for your installation.

Do not add a pipe or large wrench for leverage on a stuck or corroded valve. If it leaks, will not move, or is in doubtful condition, arrange professional attention. Do not make annual exercise of every old valve a universal task without considering its condition and the responsible professional's advice.

body.heading: Ask the question that resolves uncertainty

items.line: Which water shutoff may I operate at this property, and what should I do if that valve will not close?
Please identify the domestic shutoff, any fire-sprinkler branch, and the safe procedure for closing and restoring this supply.
Where is my unit's water isolation, who is authorized to operate it, and which emergency contact should I use after hours?

body.heading: A safe confirmation test needs context
paragraphs: If a qualified person has confirmed a test is appropriate, follow the instructions for your installation and verify the result as directed. Residual water can remain in pipes, and continued flow may have more than one explanation. Do not keep tightening a handle to chase every last drip.

Water heaters, boilers, pumps, treatment equipment, and sprinkler systems can introduce additional requirements when water is isolated or restored. This article is not a drain-down or restart procedure for those systems. Ask about them before a planned shutdown rather than assuming opening a faucet makes every installation safe.

body.heading: If water is escaping now
paragraphs: Use the confirmed occupant-operated valve only if you can reach and operate it safely. If the leak is clearly at a fixture and its correct local valve is known and safe, isolating that fixture may be appropriate while help is arranged. Otherwise call the plumber, building emergency contact, or utility as relevant.

Do not enter standing water near electrical equipment or go beneath an unstable wet ceiling to reach a valve. Move away from danger and use appropriate emergency assistance. Utility-owned valves, unfamiliar fire-system components, and inaccessible spaces are not an invitation to improvise.

body.heading: Keep a record someone can actually follow
paragraphs: Write directions such as 'utility closet beside the kitchen, lower access panel' rather than 'by the pipes.' Add a photograph of the confirmed valve in its surroundings, the responsible contact, and any limits on use. Avoid publishing sensitive access information where strangers can see it.

Review the page after plumbing work or a move. Keep it with [your home binder](/guides/how-to-make-a-home-binder), but make sure the relevant people know where it is. An accurate private record is more useful than a bright label on an unverified valve.

items.q: Is the main shutoff always inside?
items.a: No universal location applies. Construction, supply arrangement, and local practice differ. Use records and the relevant utility or building guidance to identify the correct customer-operated valve. Do not assume an outside meter or curb valve is yours to use.

items.q: What if the valve is stuck?
items.a: Stop rather than forcing it. Contact a plumber, building manager, or utility according to which valve it is. If a leak is active, explain that it is an emergency. Record the failed condition so others do not assume the shutoff is ready for use.

items.q: Can I just turn off the water heater valve?
items.a: That may isolate only the heater, not the home's cold supply or a leak elsewhere. Confirm what the valve controls. Planned isolation or restoration can also involve appliance-specific requirements, so obtain the correct instructions rather than treating a nearby handle as the main shutoff.
